slides.title: Markov Decision Processes, Policies, and Value Iteration

segments.label: Concept and boundary
segments.text: This lesson changes the question from what will happen to what an agent should do. We begin with Markov prediction, add actions and rewards, and end with value iteration. Keep model, evaluation, optimization, and audit separate: an algorithm can solve the stated model exactly while the model still omits a fact that matters in the world.

slides.title: Sequence models connect observations across time or space

segments.label: Concept and boundary
segments.text: A sequence model links observations that arrive in an order. Speech, robot localization, attention, and medical monitoring all have state that changes through time or position. The key modeling task is deciding what the state must remember so that the next-step distribution no longer needs the entire raw history.

slides.title: A Markov model starts with state, an initial distribution, and transitions

segments.label: Concept and boundary
segments.text: A Markov model needs three ingredients before any prediction is possible: a state space, an initial distribution, and transition dynamics. State says what can be true now, the initial distribution says where uncertainty begins, and the transition model says how probability mass moves from one step to the next.

Initial distribution P(X₁) Uncertainty before the sequence begins. Transition dynamics P(Xₜ|Xₜ₋₁) How the state evolves one step. TERMINOLOGY CORRECTION Reusing the same transition probabilities at every time is a time-homogeneous transition assumption. It is not required by every Markov model and is not the same as a stationary state distribution. slides.title: The Markov assumption shortens the chain-rule history

segments.label: Concept and boundary
segments.text: The Markov assumption is a conditional-independence claim, not a claim that the past never mattered. Its role is to summarize every relevant effect of the past inside the present state. That shortens the chain rule from a growing history to repeated local factors, which makes representation and computation tractable.

visualDesign.focusPhrase: The Markov assumption is a conditional-independence claim, not

focuses.phrase: The Markov assumption is a conditional-independence claim, not
focuses.label: Concept and boundary

segments.label: Read the visible model
segments.text: Now connect that idea to the exact visible evidence. X₁ leads to X₂ leads to X₃ leads to X₄ leads to … 1 · CHAIN RULE IDENTITY P(x₁:ₜ) = P(x₁) ∏i=2T P(xᵢ | x₁:ᵢ₋₁) Valid for every joint distribution. 2 · FIRST-ORDER ASSUMPTION Xᵢ ⟂ X₁:ᵢ₋₂ | Xᵢ₋₁ The present state screens off earlier history. 3 · MARKOV FACTORIZATION P(x₁:ₜ) = P(x₁) ∏i=2T P(xᵢ | xᵢ₋₁) A modeling assumption makes the factors local. IN-CLASS CHECK Which line is a probability identity, and which line introduces the Markov modeling assumption? slides.title: Given the present, earlier history adds no information about the next state

segments.label: Concept and boundary
segments.text: Read this independence statement carefully. Once the present state is known, earlier states should add no information about the next state. If an omitted variable such as battery level or traffic phase still changes the next-step probabilities, then the chosen state is not Markov and must be repaired.

visualDesign.focusPhrase: Read this independence statement carefully. Once the present

IMPLIED PROPERTY past ⟂ future | present Knowing the present blocks information flow along the chain. PROOF IDEA factor, cancel, normalize For example, P(X₁|X₂,X₃,X₄)=P(X₁|X₂). CORRECTION TO THE ORIGINAL WORDING Past and future are conditionally independent given the present; they are not “independent of the present.” Read symbols as named quantities, trace each arrow as a dependency or transition, and verify that every probability or value has a stated conditioning context.

slides.title: An unrolled first-order chain is a Bayesian network

segments.label: Concept and boundary
segments.text: An unrolled first-order Markov chain is also a Bayesian network. Each time step is a node, and each local conditional distribution is a factor. This bridge matters because the same graphical-model reasoning from Lesson twelve now explains a sequence: d-separation, factorization, and conditional independence still do the work.

slides.title: One transition model has three equivalent representations

segments.label: Concept and boundary
segments.text: The weather example shows one transition model in three equivalent forms: a conditional-probability table, a directed state graph, and a matrix. They must agree row by row. Each representation supports a different task, so translating among them is a useful error-detection skill rather than decorative notation.

segments.label: Concept and boundary

slides.title: Forward prediction repeatedly applies the same transition operator

segments.label: Concept and boundary
segments.text: Forward prediction repeats the same transition operator. Multiply the current distribution by the transition matrix to obtain the next distribution, then feed that result into the following step. Watch probability mass spread and stabilize while remembering that the result remains conditional on the modeled dynamics.

slides.title: A stationary distribution is a fixed point—not a universal convergence promise

segments.label: Concept and boundary
segments.text: A stationary distribution is a fixed point of the transition operator. Starting from that distribution leaves it unchanged after one step. Do not turn this definition into a universal convergence promise: periodic, reducible, or otherwise poorly behaved chains may fail to converge uniquely from every starting state.

WEATHER EQUATIONS pi (sun)=.9 pi (sun)+.3 pi (rain) pi (rain)=.1 pi (sun)+.7 pi (rain) pi (sun)+ pi (rain)=1 SOLVE pi (sun)=¾ pi (rain)=¼ CONVERGENCE CONDITION This chain converges because it is finite, irreducible, and aperiodic. A stationary distribution alone does not guarantee convergence from every start. slides.title: A Markov chain predicts; an MDP adds choices and consequences

segments.label: Concept and boundary
segments.text: A Markov chain predicts what state comes next under fixed dynamics. A Markov decision process adds an action choice, and actions change the transition distribution and reward consequences. That is the conceptual boundary between passive prediction and control.

slides.title: An MDP is the tuple ⟨S, A, P, R, γ⟩

segments.label: Concept and boundary
segments.text: The MDP tuple contains states, actions, transition probabilities, rewards, and a discount factor. Each symbol answers a different modeling question. A complete solution requires all five, and each is an assumption that can be challenged with evidence.

visualDesign.focusPhrase: The MDP tuple contains states, actions, transition probabilities

focuses.phrase: The MDP tuple contains states, actions, transition probabilities
focuses.label: Concept and boundary

segments.label: Read the visible model
segments.text: Now connect that idea to the exact visible evidence. S States Information the model treats as sufficient for predicting the next transition and reward. A Actions Choices available to the agent; A(s) may depend on the state. P Transitions P(s′|s,a), a probability distribution over next states. R Reward R(s,a,s′), the immediate scalar signal used by the objective. gamma Discount 0≤ gamma <1 for continuing discounted tasks; weights later rewards. MARKOV REQUIREMENT Given the modeled state and current action, the distribution of next state and reward must not require additional history. If it does, the state representation is insufficient. slides.title: Actions change transition distributions; they do not guarantee outcomes

segments.label: Concept and boundary
segments.text: An action does not normally determine the next state. It selects a probability distribution over next states. In the gridworld, moving right can reach the intended cell, slip sideways, or leave the agent in place. Planning must average over those outcomes rather than pretending the most likely one is certain.

slides.title: Reward is the formal objective—not a label for what humans value

segments.label: Concept and boundary
segments.text: Reward is the formal objective supplied to the agent. It is not automatically the same as human value, safety, or long-term usefulness. Reward design is therefore both mathematical and socio-technical: specify what is measured, stress-test shortcuts, constrain unacceptable behavior, and monitor for gaming.

segments.label: Concept and boundary

slides.title: Policy evaluation averages; optimal control maximizes

segments.label: Concept and boundary
segments.text: Policy evaluation averages over the actions chosen by a fixed policy. Optimal control replaces that policy-weighted action average with a maximum over actions. The immediate reward remains; only the decision rule changes. This distinction prevents a common error of maximizing the wrong part of the equation.

slides.title: Value iteration applies Bellman optimality synchronously until change is small

segments.label: Concept and boundary

slides.title: A small Bellman residual is solver evidence, not real-world validation

segments.label: Concept and boundary
segments.text: A small Bellman residual is evidence about the numerical solver. It does not validate the reward function, transition model, state representation, or deployment setting. Keep solver convergence and real-world validity as separate claims with separate tests.

visualDesign.focusPhrase: A small Bellman residual is evidence about the

focuses.phrase: A small Bellman residual is evidence about the
focuses.label: Concept and boundary

segments.label: Read the visible model
segments.text: Now connect that idea to the exact visible evidence. DISCOUNTED FINITE MDP The Bellman optimality operator is a gamma -contraction With 0≤ gamma <1 and bounded rewards, repeated optimality backups converge to a unique V*. The residual Δ measures numerical change under the model. Iteration rule Stop after a fixed compute budget; simple, but no direct accuracy guarantee. Residual rule Stop when max state change is below a chosen tolerance. Policy stability Monitor whether greedy actions stop changing; ties need care. DO NOT CONFLATE ERRORS Small iteration error does not imply small transition-model error, reward-specification error, or deployment risk.
